source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: San Juan Mountains; Animas River; Baker's Park
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, March 2, 1868
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 619
summary: Prospectors, probably sanctioned by Territorial Governor McCook, trespassed into the 1868 reservation in 1870 and found rich mineral deposits; by 1871 a stamp mill and scores of mining claims existed on Ute land in direct violation of the treaty.
verbatim_quote: Scores of individuals filed claims on Indian land
sources_cited_by_source: McCook quotes from Annual Report of the Dept. of the Interior 1869 p.711 (n33) and Manypenny, Our Indian Wards (1880) p.404 (n34)
federal_account_contrast: Royce frames 566 as a cession by agreement; this shows the mining takeover preceded and forced the cession.
map_implication: Annotate Royce 566 as occupied by illegal trespass (1870-1873) before any cession; add timeline layer of trespass before treaty.
notes: PSL says McCook 'probably' sanctioned the trespass; that inference is the authors'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1872 San Juan cession negotiation (failed)
summary: Federal commissioners admitted trespassers were violating the 1868 treaty but said nothing could be done and the Utes should cede the mines to avoid bloodshed. Ouray refused to sell and demanded removal of intruders; the council ended without a cession.
verbatim_quote: it would be to the Utes' advantage to give up the mining districts so that they could avoid conflicts and avert possible bloodshed
federal_account_contrast: Shows the US openly conceded treaty breach and offered cession as the remedy for its own non-enforcement.
map_implication: Note on Royce 566: Ute refusal of 1872, and conceded US non-enforcement of 1868 treaty.
notes: Interested parties present included Otto Mears and McCook's brother-in-law J.B. Thompson; interpreter Curtis previously accused of selling Ute rations to Mears.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Los Pinos; Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory; Washington DC
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 36 (1874) (cited via US v. Southern Ute, 402 U.S. 159)
summary: Commissioner Felix Brunot used Ouray's captive son (taken by Lakota, traded to Arapaho) as a bargaining tool, promising recovery in return for Ouray urging the San Juan cession. The boy was never delivered; the youth produced in Washington was disowned by Ouray.
verbatim_quote: Brunot was content to exploit this belief without even knowing whether the boy was alive or dead.
sources_cited_by_source: Hafen, Efforts to Recover the Stolen Son of Chief Ouray, Colorado Magazine XVI(2) 1939 p.60 (n41)
federal_account_contrast: Official report states no inducements were used; PSL documents a captive child used as leverage.
map_implication: Flag Royce 566 cession as obtained with leverage over a captive child of the lead signatory.
notes: Brunot's 1901 account that the youth was Ouray's son is uncorroborated per PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 43d Cong., 1st Sess. (1873) pp.453-467
summary: The Utes would cede only existing mines and mountain land, not farming valleys; Brunot refused a mines-only sale. Ouray's letter of Sept 13 says they would sell 'mountainland' but not valleys. Utes understood they retained hunting rights and had sold only mining areas.
verbatim_quote: We are perfectly willing to sell our mountainland, and hope the miners will find heaps of gold and silver
sources_cited_by_source: Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1873, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. pp.454, 467 (n35-37)
federal_account_contrast: Royce draws a clean 60x100 mile cession; Ute understanding was a narrower mines-only sale with retained hunting rights.
map_implication: Show Ute-understood scope (mining districts only) vs. drawn Royce 566; mark retained hunting rights over 566.
notes: Approx. 4 million acres per PSL narrative; 3.7 million per Supreme Court in 402 U.S. 159.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Uncompahgre Park; Gunnison and San Miguel rivers; south end of reservation
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 43d Cong., 1st Sess. p.454
summary: Brunot's own report says the cession took mineral country of over 60 by 100 miles, while Uncompahgre Park, the Gunnison and San Miguel Rivers and the agricultural and grazing lands on the south end were reserved to the Indians. Utes were to receive $25,000 per year in perpetuity.
verbatim_quote: The Uncompagre Park, the Gunnison and San Miguel Rivers, and the agricultural and grazing lands on the south end of the present reservation are reserved to the Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: Brunot report, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. (n38)
federal_account_contrast: Adds the reserved areas inside/adjacent to 566 that were later taken anyway.
map_implication: Draw Uncompahgre Park and the southern agricultural lands as land expressly reserved in 1873.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: Article 6
summary: Brunot stated no presents or extra promises were made, yet Article 6 gave Ouray a $1,000 annual salary for ten years while he remained at peace and 'head chief of the Utes'.
verbatim_quote: No presents were given to influence them, and no promises were made other than those mentioned in this report
sources_cited_by_source: H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. p.453 (n39)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents the salary as a routine clause; PSL frames it as an inducement to the key signatory.
map_implication: Note on Royce 566: payment to principal signatory written into the agreement.
notes: A separate claim (Sidney Jocknick) that Mears arranged the signing is flagged by PSL as uncorroborated.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: After signing, the Indian Bureau told the Utes the $25,000 annuity would not go to them but would be spent at agents' discretion; a request to buy horses was answered that they needed a schoolhouse.
verbatim_quote: was to go into the hands of government agents and be dispersed according to the discretion of such agents
sources_cited_by_source: Rocky Mountain News, Nov 1, 1873 (quoted in text)
federal_account_contrast: Changes the meaning of the consideration after signature.
map_implication: Note that the 1873 consideration was controlled by agents, not paid to the nation.
notes: Newspaper report; 'supposedly' in PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Little Annie mine, San Juan country
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: Per an 1873 Colorado newspaper, Ute Agent Charles Adams, while in Washington with the Ute delegation, sold two-thirds of the Little Annie gold mine (on trespassed Ute land) for half a million dollars.
verbatim_quote: has made a sale of two-thirds of the Little Annie gold mine in the San Juan country
federal_account_contrast: The agent charged with protecting Ute interests profited from trespass during the cession negotiation.
map_implication: Conflict-of-interest note on Royce 566 negotiation.
notes: Single newspaper source, unnamed; needs verification.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, 1868
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 619
summary: Investigator found Agent Jabez Trask held $25,000 of Ute appropriations locked in a Denver bank while refusing to issue food.
verbatim_quote: Trask had $25,000 of Ute appropriations money locked up in a Denver bank
federal_account_contrast: Annuity withholding not reflected in treaty text.
map_implication: Add to annuity non-performance record for 1868 treaty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: The greatest portion of the San Juan cession came from southern band territory; the southern bands felt they had been tricked into signing, refused to come to Los Pinos even for rations, and rejected the first-year Brunot payments, accusing the Tabeguache of manipulating them.
verbatim_quote: The southern Utes felt they had been tricked into signing the compact
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats 566 as ceded by the confederated Utes; the bands whose land it mostly was rejected it.
map_implication: Flag Royce 566 as contested by the southern bands whose territory it mainly was.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Brunot Agreement 1873; Executive order 1876; Act of May 14, 1884
summary: Uncompahgre Park was expressly reserved in 1873, but a government surveyor (Miller) contracted the boundaries and included it in the cession; settlers moved in. Grant's 1876 executive order restored about sixteen square miles but the military could not enforce it. After the Utes were removed, the Act of May 14, 1884 returned the park to public domain.
verbatim_quote: In 1876, President Grant had issued a special order restoring sixteen square miles of the Uncompahgre Park to the Utes
sources_cited_by_source: Smith, ARCIA 1876 p.19 (n42); ICC Docket 327 findings
federal_account_contrast: Not a treaty cession at all: taken by survey error and statute after removal.
map_implication: Map Uncompahgre Park (10,240 acres) separately as reserved land taken by statute 1884, never ceded; do not color as part of Royce 566 cession.
notes: PSL p.455 says the surveyor 'deliberately' included it; p.420 calls it an 'error'. Internal inconsistency.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Los Pinos; White River Agency; Rawlins depot
instrument: Treaty 1868; Brunot Agreement 1873
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 45th Cong., 2d Sess. (1877) p.442
summary: By 1877 the US was about $90,000 behind on Ute annuities. Agent Danforth reported White River supplies were under half of need, with no clothing, blankets or tools for nearly two years and flour sitting at Rawlins.
verbatim_quote: The annuities and supplies furnished these Indians amount to not over one-half that required for their support.
sources_cited_by_source: ARCIA 1877, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 45th Cong. 2d Sess. p.442 (n43)
federal_account_contrast: Documents non-performance of treaty consideration.
map_implication: Annuity default layer for 1868/1873 obligations.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1878 congressional authorization to negotiate consolidation at White River (act not named by PSL); 1878 Ute Commission
instrument_cite: H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 84, 45th Cong., 3d Sess. (1879) pp.1-2
summary: Commissioner Hayt proposed consolidating all Utes on a 728,320-acre reservation near White River and extinguishing title to the southern reservation; the southern bands categorically refused and no agreement was ratified.
verbatim_quote: uniting them upon one diminished reservation
federal_account_contrast: Shows pre-Meeker federal intent to diminish the reservation.
map_implication: Context note; no boundary change.
notes: PSL attributes the authorizing language to Secretary Schurz; it reads as statutory text. Exact 1878 act not named by PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: PSL argues Nathan Meeker was placed at White River through Pitkin, Teller, Evans and Byers, men with mining and railroad interests in removing the Utes. Meeker withheld rations from Utes who would not farm on his terms.
verbatim_quote: Meeker began to withhold rations from those who would not work according to his instructions
federal_account_contrast: Federal record frames Meeker as a civilizing agent; PSL frames appointment as a setup.
map_implication: Context note for 1880 removal.
notes: The 'setup' thesis is the authors' interpretation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: Governor Pitkin telegraphed that White River Utes had burned 'millions of dollars of timber' and urged removal to Indian Territory; Major Thornburgh investigated and found no such activity, and settlers gave statements that the Utes had set no fires.
verbatim_quote: so far as I can learn no one attributes the burning of timber to these Indians
sources_cited_by_source: Colorado Daily Chieftain July 8, 1879; Thornburgh report to Crook July 27, 1879 (no endnote)
federal_account_contrast: State fabrication used to build a removal case.
map_implication: Note: state-generated false accusations preceded 1879-1881 removal.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
nations: White River Utes; Canalla (Johnson); Nicaagat (Captain Jack)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 83, 46th Cong., 2d Sess. (White River Ute Commission)
summary: Meeker plowed Ute horse pasture, then telegraphed a false claim of assault by Canalla; troops were sent. Thornburgh agreed to halt, then crossed Milk Creek, the reservation's northern boundary, with his whole column on Sept 29, 1879, triggering the battle.
verbatim_quote: The Indians seem to consider the advance of troops as a declaration of real war.
sources_cited_by_source: White River Ute Commission evidence, H.R. Exec. Doc. 83 pp.7, 37-38, 55 (n50-53)
federal_account_contrast: Federal and popular narrative calls it the 'Meeker Massacre' and an 'outbreak'; record shows troops entered the reservation contrary to agreement.
map_implication: Mark Milk Creek battle site (Sept 29, 1879) as US military entry onto the 1868 reservation.
notes: Who fired first is unresolved per PSL; Jack said soldiers did.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: After news of Milk Creek reached the agency, Ute warriors killed Meeker and the male employees and took three women and two children captive. PSL notes 12 soldiers killed and 43 wounded at Milk Creek.
verbatim_quote: All male agency employees were swiftly dispatched
federal_account_contrast: Included because the event was the stated justification for removal of all White River and Uncompahgre Utes.
map_implication: Event marker; not a land-taking instrument itself.
notes: Violence by Utes; recorded for context, not as a massacre of Natives.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: Two companies of Colorado militia were dispatched with the governor's orders to kill all Indians found off the reservation.
verbatim_quote: orders from the governor to kill all Indians found off the reservation
federal_account_contrast: State-ordered lethal force not in federal treaty record.
map_implication: State-action marker, Colorado, Oct 1879.
notes: Needs a primary source for the order.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: White River Ute Commission (Hatch, Adams, Ouray)
instrument_cite: H.R. Misc. Doc. No. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess.; H.R. Exec. Doc. 83
summary: Adams first reported the captive women suffered 'no indignities' but later pressed them, after private meetings with Pitkin, to allege rape. The commission then named 12 men on the women's statements although they admitted they had witnessed no killings.
verbatim_quote: It is clear from his own testimony that Adams put pressure on Price to say she had been violated.
sources_cited_by_source: House Misc. Doc. 38 pp.10-11 (n58); H.R. Exec. Doc. 83 p.12 (n59)
federal_account_contrast: Official record presents the rape findings as fact; PSL argues they were manufactured to justify removal.
map_implication: Note in removal record: evidentiary basis of commission contested.
notes: PSL interpretation of motive is inferential ('quite probable').

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
instrument_cite: Treaty with the Ute 1868 Art. 17, 15 Stat. 619
summary: The Uncompahgre Utes, who took no part at Milk Creek or White River, were made to share the punishment and removal. PSL notes this contradicts Article 17 of the 1868 treaty, which preserves benefits for any Indian who remains at peace.
verbatim_quote: We are Uncompahgre; they are White River Utes, and not under my immediate control.
sources_cited_by_source: Ouray statement: 'No citation information available' (PSL); Art. 17 of 1868 treaty quoted
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats the 1880 cession as a negotiated agreement; PSL shows collective punishment contrary to treaty terms.
map_implication: Flag Uncompahgre portion of Royce 616 as taken as collective punishment contrary to 1868 Art. 17.
notes: Ouray quote has no citation per PSL itself.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Treaty 1868 (US recognition of title)
instrument_cite: ARCIA 1879
summary: Commissioner Hayt's own 1879 report acknowledged the Utes held good title to 12,000,000 acres in Colorado by solemn treaty, which must be honored 'whether convenient or otherwise'.
verbatim_quote: the Ute Indians have a good and sufficient title to 12,000,000 acres of land in Colorado
federal_account_contrast: Federal official contemporaneously affirmed Ute title just before the removal agreement.
map_implication: Use as quote on the 1868 reservation polygon.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Grand River near mouth of Gunnison River, Colorado
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
instrument_cite: Act of June 15, 1880 (21 Stat. 199, cite not given by PSL)
summary: The 1880 agreement promised the Uncompahgre a reservation on agricultural land on the Grand River near the mouth of the Gunnison 'if a sufficient quantity' were found. Commissioner Otto Mears, who saw the land's value, falsely reported it insufficient, backed by commissioners McMorris and Russell, so the Uncompahgre were sent to Utah.
verbatim_quote: The Uncompahgre Utes agree to remove to and settle upon agricultural lands on Grand River, near the mouth of the Gunnison River, in Colorado, if a sufficient quantity of agricultural land shall be found there
sources_cited_by_source: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, 1880 (n22, n67); Kirkwood letter to Committee on Public Lands, 1882
federal_account_contrast: Federal record says no suitable land existed; PSL says the finding was false.
map_implication: Draw the promised Grand/Gunnison confluence reservation area (Grand Junction vicinity) as land promised in 1880 and withheld on a false report.
notes: Boundary of the promised area was never surveyed; only described as vicinity of the confluence.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
summary: The 1880 agreement provided the Southern Utes would settle on unoccupied agricultural lands on the La Plata River in Colorado, or if insufficient, in its vicinity in New Mexico. Manypenny found the La Plata insufficient after two surveys; the move never happened.
verbatim_quote: The Southern Utes agree to remove to and settle upon the unoccupied agricultural lands on the La Plata River, in Colorado
sources_cited_by_source: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, 1880 (n67, ch.2 n7)
federal_account_contrast: Promised La Plata allotments were never delivered.
map_implication: Show La Plata River lands as promised 1880, not delivered.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
nations: Uncompahgre Utes; Southern Utes; White River Utes
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
instrument_cite: Act of June 15, 1880 (three-fourths adult male ratification requirement)
summary: Ratification required signatures of three-fourths of Ute adult men. Most Uncompahgre and Southern Utes refused; Ouray died in Aug 1880 without signing the ratification (per Conetah). Commissioner Otto Mears then paid Ute men two dollars per signature. Chairman Manypenny refused to approve and Mears was ordered to Washington, but Secretary Kirkwood dropped charges and reimbursed Mears for the bribes.
verbatim_quote: Otto Mears... began to bribe the Ute men for their signatures at two dollars apiece.
sources_cited_by_source: Conetah, A History of the Northern Ute People (1982) (Native-authored, Uintah-Ouray Ute Tribe)
federal_account_contrast: Royce 616 is shown as a ratified cession; the three-fourths consent was obtained by bribery that the US reimbursed.
map_implication: Flag Royce 616 as consent procured by bribery; note the federal reimbursement of the bribes.
notes: Native-authored source (Conetah). Death of Kaniache by lightning also cited as factor. PSL does not give the final signature count.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: White River, Colorado to Uintah Reservation, Utah
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
summary: The 1880 agreement expelled the White River Utes to agricultural lands on the Uintah Reservation in Utah; by May 1881 most had gone. Some merged with Southern Utes.
verbatim_quote: The White River Utes agree to remove to and settle upon agricultural lands on the Uintah Reservation in Utah.
map_implication: Removal route White River to Uintah; mark 1881.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
summary: The 1880 agreement paid $500 a year from Ute monies to the Meeker women and Mrs. Price and other payments to families of employees; Captain Jack served a year at Fort Leavenworth though never named by the women.
verbatim_quote: a clause was included that would annually pay five hundred dollars to the Meeker women and Mrs. Price from the Ute monies
federal_account_contrast: Ute treaty funds diverted to reparations.
map_implication: Note on 1880 consideration.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Uncompahgre River valley to Uintah/Ouray Reservation, Utah (350 miles)
instrument: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Ute, March 6, 1880, ratified by Act of June 15, 1880
summary: The Uncompahgre refused to leave. Col. Ranald Mackenzie established a cantonment near Los Pinos, turned field artillery on a group that tried to resist, surrounded the people and gave them 24 hours. About 1,400 people were marched 350 miles; the last left Sept 7, 1881. Mears held the contract for the removal road and new agency.
verbatim_quote: the Utes had 24 hours to prepare for departure
sources_cited_by_source: Gunnison Review July 1881; Conetah; Gen. Pope quote via 'several sources'
federal_account_contrast: Federal account records a voluntary agreement; actual removal was by force over refusal.
map_implication: Draw Uncompahgre removal route (Sept 1881) and label forced military removal.
notes: Gen. Pope quote is given without endnote.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Colorado House Bill No. 178 (1881)
summary: Representative John Coulter introduced a bill offering $25 from the state treasury for each Indian or skunk scalp.
verbatim_quote: any person who shall produce the scalp of any Indian or skunk found in this State, shall receive a reward or premium of twenty-five (25) dollars
federal_account_contrast: State-level exterminationist action absent from federal record.
map_implication: Statewide context marker, 1881.
notes: PSL does not say whether the bill passed. Verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
nations: White River Utes; Uncompahgre Utes; Uintah
instrument: Brunot Agreement 1873 (hunting rights)
summary: Exiled Utes kept returning to hunt in Colorado, insisting they never gave up hunting rights; dendrochronology shows over half of recorded Ute encampment sites in NW Colorado were used after removal.
verbatim_quote: They insisted that they had not given up their right to hunt in their ancestral homelands through any treaty or agreement.
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats cession as complete; Utes maintained retained usufruct rights.
map_implication: Overlay retained off-reservation hunting claim on Royce 566/616.
notes: Dendrochronology claim needs source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: South Montezuma Creek, Blue Mountains, Utah
summary: Cowboys working for powerful cattlemen seized Ute horses from a band holding agency hunting passes and shot a Ute man; Sixth Cavalry and about 80 armed volunteers pursued the band (Soldier Crossing fight).
verbatim_quote: The cowboy precipitously shot the Ute man.
sources_cited_by_source: McPherson & Hurst, The Fight at Soldier Crossing, 1884, Utah Historical Quarterly 70(3) 2002 (n2)
map_implication: Event marker.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: White River public domain, Garfield County; near Meeker, Colorado
summary: Garfield County Sheriff Kendall's posse burned Chipeta's camp; later posse, volunteers and Colorado National Guard attacked the Utes as they returned toward Utah. Eight Utes were killed including a small child and an infant; volunteers stole about 600 horses and 2,500 sheep. Misnamed 'Colorow's War'.
verbatim_quote: Eight Ute People had been killed, including a small child and an infant.
sources_cited_by_source: Conetah 1982 p.118 (n3, n5); Denver Public Library, Colorow and the Ute Aftermath, 2022 (n4)
federal_account_contrast: Popular history calls it an Indian war; it was a state-led attack on hunters exercising claimed Brunot rights.
map_implication: Add 1887 massacre marker near Meeker/White River.
notes: Four whites died. Exact location ('bend in the river') not given.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Gilsonite Strip, near Fort Duchesne, Utah
instrument: Act of May 24, 1888 (Gilsonite Strip)
summary: After mining claims were filed on the reservation in 1886, Congress removed a 7,000-acre strip from the Uintah and Ouray reservation and restored it to public domain; signatures were obtained despite much Ute protest.
verbatim_quote: the U.S. Congress passed an act that removed a 7,000-acre strip of land and restored it to the public domain
federal_account_contrast: Utah land; outside Colorado scope but part of Ute dispossession.
map_implication: If Utah included, draw Gilsonite Strip 1888 as statutory taking.
notes: Utah lands.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1888 Southern Ute removal agreement (S. 1916, Bowen); S. 769 (Teller, 1885)
summary: Colorado senators pushed bills to remove the Southern Utes; in 1887-88, 274 signatures were obtained (242 required) for removal to a Utah reservation, but Congress defeated it under Utah cattle lobbying.
verbatim_quote: The signatures of 242 adult male tribal members of the three Southern Ute bands were required. By November of 1888, 274 signatures had been obtained.
map_implication: Context; failed removal.
notes: Text simultaneously quotes an 1888 RMN article saying the commission failed to obtain a treaty; inconsistent with 274 signatures.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
nations: Southern Utes (Mouache, Capote); Weeminuche (Ute Mountain Ute)
place: Ute strip, SW Colorado (15 x 110 miles); Towaoc
instrument: Hunter Act, Act of February 20, 1895
instrument_cite: 28 Stat. 677 (cite not given by PSL)
summary: The Hunter Act opened the Southern Ute strip to homesteading and sale. Mouache and Capote took allotments; the Weeminuche under Ignacio refused allotment and moved west to Towaoc. Many allotments were later sold. Final Southern Ute boundaries set 1899.
verbatim_quote: In 1895 the Hunter Act was passed opening up the Ute strip to homesteading and sale to non-Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: Southern Ute Indian Tribe website, History (n8)
federal_account_contrast: Royce 617 drawn as cession; tribal account frames it as opening of a reservation remnant.
map_implication: Label Royce 617 as reservation strip opened by statute 1895 (allotment), not a cession; mark Ute Mountain Ute refusal of allotment.
notes: Tribal (Native-authored) source quoted.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Act of Aug 1894; 1897 Act; H.R. Rep. No. 2967, 51st Cong. 1st Sess. (1890)
summary: Acting Commissioner Belt opined the government need not seek Uncompahgre consent because their Utah reservation was never intended to be permanent. The 1894 act required Utes to pay $1.25 per acre for allotments from their Colorado land proceeds; the 1897 act opened unallotted land with no compensation; 83 allotments made May 1898 over protest.
verbatim_quote: the Government may not be in duty bound to submit the question for the consent of the Indians
